newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds fall on fear of more rate hikes.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds fall on fear of more rate hikes.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks and bonds closed lower Tuesday as Wall Street briefly cheered an interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve but then quickly worried that further hikes could depress economic growth.
The dollar rose against most major currencies as higher rates make yields on U.S. investments more attractive.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 29.08 points at 6,876.17. But in the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,295 to 1,161 on active volume of 480 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

In a widely anticipated move, the Fed raised the key federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point to 5.50 percent -- the first increase since Feb. 1, 1995 -- in an effort to stay a step ahead of inflation. The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.

Some commercial banks wasted no time reacting to the Fed's tightening. Citibank, Banc One Corp. and Central Fidelity Bancorp raised their prime lending rates to 8.50 percent from 8.25 percent, which will eventually boost the lending rates for home equity loans, adjustable mortgages and credit cards.
Blue-chip stocks initially jumped on the Fed's decision, which was announced at mid-afternoon but the so-called "relief rally" quickly evaporated.
Traders said even though the market had expected the Fed to raise rates, there was some concern that this might be the first in a series of hikes.
"It's still a bump in rates and maybe there's another bump to come," said Frank Calta, director of trading at Anvil Institutional Services.
Added Eric Miller, chief investment office at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, "Once the Fed has signalled a change in policy, it means the market should be on its guard."
Wall Street will be closely following economic indicators to determine if more rate increases may be coming.
"I would guess the market is going to mark time, stay in a trading range until it gets a better sense of what is going to follow," Miller said.

In the bond market, the key 30-year Treasury bond lost more than one-half point, sending its yield up to 6.97 percent from Monday's close of 6.92 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
"If (the Fed) does a second (rate hike), that's when people will get nervous," said Kevin Haggerty, manager of equity trading at Fidelity Capital Markets.
The dollar rose to 1.6903 German marks and 123.70 Japanese yen late Tuesday from 1.6880 marks and 122.85 yen late Monday.
June gold at the Commodity Exchange ended $2.50 lower at $350.50 an ounce, as the Fed's rate hike reduced demand for the precious metal, a hedge against inflation.

Coffee futures soared amid a lack of selling interest from Latin American producers. At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for delivery in May closed 16.40 cents a pound higher at 179.30 cents.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean futures rose on news of a fire at the key Brazilian port of Paranagua. That fed concern that soybean exports from Brazil would slow and U.S. exports would receive a boost.
May soybeans ended 10-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $8.42.
May wheat rose 3 cents a bushel to $3.89-1/2 after weekly crop condition reports on Monday indicated dry weather was posing a threat to the young winter wheat crop in Texas and Oklahoma.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 blue chip share index finished 55.9 points higher at 4,270.7, just below the day's best levels. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average finished 395.79 points, or 2.19 percent, higher at 18,439.61.
